div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Understanding food webs is a central question in ecology (Montoya and Solé, 2002). Predator-prey interactions have long captured researchers' attention because of the important impacts that these interactions have both on prey and predator population dynamics and on the functioning of the complete ecosystem (Lima, 1998). The selection of a particular prey is a complex decision process that results from integrating factors such as prey size, density, and availability (Griffiths, 1975;Symondson, 2002). Direct observations of feeding events are often difficult in the field and diets are studied conventionally by the morphological identification of remains in faeces which many times is a challenging task due the effect of mastication and digestion processes on these remains.

In recent times molecular and particularly, PCRbased techniques have proven to be highly effective and versatile for studying diets and are likely to rapidly displace other approaches (Symondson, 2002;Carter et al., 2006). PCR-based techniques target preys DNA in predators' faeces. Nevertheless, detecting and amplifying degraded or semi-digested DNA is not always an easy task mainly due to the presence in faeces of both reaction inhibitors and multiple DNA templates. Besides, due to its higher proportion, the predator's DNA can swamp the result of the PCR amplification, although this problem can normally be avoided using species or groupspecific primers that exclusively target prey DNA sequences (King et al., 2008). As a result, prey identification through the amplification of the prey's DNA is now possible even from highly degraded samples such as faeces, guts content or regurgitates (Zeale et al., 2011). This possibility is changing the perspective of diet studies, and in fact the approach has allowed identifying prey species in a variety of biological remains from spiders (Agustí et al., 2003) to pinnipeds (Parsons et al., 2005), Macarony penguins (Deagle et al., 2007) or bats (Clare et al., 2009;Zeale et al., 2011;Alberdi et al., 2012). Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has been widely employed in species identification due to its relative abundance and high mutation rate, which facilitates the distinction between species, even between closely related species (Brown et al., 1979). For this

The molecular identification of prey in faeces is an efficient non-invasive technique to study diet which requires both a satisfactory method of DNA extraction and the design of specific primers to selectively amplify prey's DNA. In this study we evaluated and compared the efficiency of two total DNA extraction methods and five primer pairs for the molecular identification of birds from scats, in particular from the giant noctule bat (Nyctalus lasiopterus). A modified DNA stool Mini Kit of Qiagen was tested against a modified silica method with a guanidinium thiocianate (GuSCN) applied after freezing and pulverizing the samples. We also checked two published vertebrate-and bird-generalist primer pairs and three bird-specific primer pairs designed by us (two pairs targeting the cytochrome b and one the cytochrome oxidase subunit I genes) that amplified shorter DNA fragments. The results show that pulverizing the scat remains before extraction was a very important step, presumably facilitating access to the well preserved DNA located inside the rachis of the feathers. The combination of our bird-specific designed primers showed a higher amplification rate than the generalist primers and allowed successful bird identification from the feathers excreted by the giant noctule bat in all the scat samples analyzed, independent of the preservation method used (dried and frozen). These methodological improvements will allow not only the study of the avian diet composition of the enigmatic giant noctule, but the extension of this methodology to other bird predators such as raptors.

reason, mtDNA markers have been widely used in diet studies, which usually rely on the partial or complete sequencing of genes such as cytochrome b (cyt b) or cytochrome oxidase subunit I (COI). Particularly, the use of COI is increasing owing primarily to its adoption by the Barcode for Life Consortium (Tobe et al., 2010). DNA barcoding employs sequence diversity in short, standardized gene regions to aid species identification and discovery in large assemblages of species. The Barcode of Life Data System (BOLD) -www. barcodinglife.orgprovides an integrated bioinformatics platform that supports all phases of the analytical pathway from specimen collection to a tightly validated barcode library (Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007).

Bats typically show a wide variety of diets that range from arthropods, vertebrates, fruits, nectar and pollen, to leaves and even blood. This wide diversification of diet is striking in comparison to other mammal groups or even vertebrates (Altringham, 2011). In temperate regions, bats are mainly insectivorous and they are major consumers of nocturnal insects many of which are economically important pests (Agosta, 2002).

Diet studies of insectivorous bats traditionally relied on the morphological identification in faeces of microscopic remains -primarily fragments of arthropod cuticles -resulting from chewing prey into tiny pieces. These remains do not allow taxonomic identification normally further than to Order, which usually provides only a gross estimate of the number and diversity of insects eaten, hence providing only a reduced perspective on the real diet (Whi t aker et al., 2009;Zeale et al., 2011). On the other hand, the use of molecular techniques has increased the accuracy of prey identification in bat diet studies even to the species level (Zeale et al., 2011).

The giant noctule bat (Nyctalus lasiopterus) was found to be the first Palaearctic bat to feed on flying passerines after the discovery of feathers in their faecal pellets (Dondini and Vergari, 2000;Ibáñez et al., 2001). Small birds are preyed upon during their fall and spring migrations (Ibáñez et al., 2001). This seasonal feeding switch from insects to birds was later confirmed by stable isotopes analysis. The signature of the bat's blood isotopic composition peaked during Spring and Autumn, coinciding with the periods in which feathers appear in the droppings and matching the birds migration patterns (Popa-Lisseanu et al., 2007). Never theless, species composition of the avian diet of this bat remains unknown since almost all the remains consist on little fragments of feathers (Dondini and Vergari, 2000) that do not allow further morphological identification.

Our objectives in this research are: i) to test if different preservation methods of faecal samples and/or storage time affect DNA preservation, ii) to develop an efficient protocol for DNA extraction from bat faeces and iii) to search for diagnostic mtDNA fragments that amplifying only avian DNA against other DNAs present in the bat scats, allowing birds identification at species level.

div.head: Collection, Storage and Preservation of Faeces
div.p: For this study, we selected faecal pellets that showed presence of feathers from a total of 47 giant noctules netted either over water courses in three points across Spain (La Rioja, Malaga and Jaen), or captured as they returned to their tree roosts in a city-park in Seville. Bats were individually kept in clean cloth bags and thereafter sexed, weighed, measured, ringed and released at the site of capture. A total of 23 faecal pellets were preserved by drying in paper bags at room temperature (11 collected in 2000 and 12 in 2005), whereas another batch of 24 faecal pellets was preserved by freezing at -20ºC (13 collected in 2006 and 11 in 2009). All samples were processed in 2012.

div.head: DNA Extraction
div.p: Total DNA extraction was performed in a sterile DNA laboratory. DNA was extracted from about 0.01-0.05 g of faecal pellet unit using two different protocols: a) the Zeale et al. (2011)'s method (based on a modified DNA stool Mini Kit of Qiagen) and starting by washing the pellet, and b) the Rohland and Hof reiter (2007) silica method with guanidinium thiocianate (GuSCN), modified by first freezing the samples with liquid nitrogen and then pulverizing using two 2.5-mm diameter steel balls. Both extraction methods were used in most of scats (Table 1). DNA extracts were recovered with milli-Q water to a total volume of 60 µl. Blanks without samples (one per extraction) were systematically included to detect possible contaminations.

div.head: Primer Design and Testing
div.p: The resolution in bird identification of previously published general primers was tested against newly designed primers for fragments of cyt b and COI. We used the vertebrate generalist primer pairs M13BC-FW/BCV-RV1 for a first PCR amplification, and M13/BCV-RV2 for the products re-amplification (Alcaide et al., 2009) of a COI's final fragment of 758 bp. In addition, the bird-specific primer pair Bird-F1/COIbirdR2, used previously for bar-coding a bird community (Kerr et al., 2009), was used to amplify a COI 648 bp fragment. The diagnostic resolution of these generalist and relatively long fragments were tested against specific and short fragments of cyt b and COI obtained using newly designed primers. These primers were designed from a selection of 81 homologous cyt b and 77 COI sequences from 86 birds downloaded from GenBank (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank) and BOLD Systems (www.barcodinglife.org) and aligned with SEQUENCHER ver. 4.9 (Gene Codes Corporation, Ann Arbor, MI USA). The selection was based on a list of potential bird species that may be preyed upon by the giant noctule in the Iberian Peninsula according to their body mass (< 80 g) and wingspan (< 33 cm), following del Hoyo et al. (2004)(2005)(2006)(2007)(2008)(2009)(2010)(2011). The final list of potential prey is as follows: seven Alaudidae, three Hirundinidae, seven Motacillidae, one Troglodytidae, nine Turdidae, two Musci ca pi dae, two Regulidae, one Cis ticolidae, 23 Silviidae, one Para do xornithidae, five Paridae, one Re mizidae, one Aegithalidae, one Sittidae, one Certhiidae, one Lani idae, four Pas seridae, 10 Frin gillidae and six Emberizidae). Gen Bank accession numbers for all sequences used in this study are listed in Appendix.

Primers were designed using the software Primer3 v. 2.3.2. (Koressaar and Remm, 2007) in conserved regions and selected avoiding primer-dimer formation, self-complementarity, too low melting temperature (Tm) and incorrect internal stability profile (Rychlik, 1995). The sequences obtained with the new primers were first aligned with SEQUENCHER ver. 4.9 and then inspected using PAUP ver. 4.0.b10 (Swofford, 2001) to assure that they represented unique haplotypes and that we were able to correctly distinguish each of the species within the set of birds.

div.head: PCR Amplification and Sequencing
div.p: The 47 DNA extracts were amplified in a 28 µl total volume consisting of: 3 µl 10 X NH4 buffer, 0.8 µl 50 mM MgCl 2 , 5 µg bovine serum albumin (BSA), 1.2 µg dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), 0.2 mM dNTP mix, 0.75 µl 10 mM forward and reverse primer and 0.16 µl 5 u/µl BIOTAQ DNA polymerase. Purified water was added to complete the 28 µl volume and 3 µl of DNA extract were added up to a final volume of 31 µl.

The PCR thermocycling included a 3 min initial denaturation step at 94ºC followed by 35 cycles of 1 min at 94ºC, 1 min at annealing temperatures between 45-55ºC (depending on primers), 1 min at 72ºC followed by a final extension of 5 min. at 72ºC. PCR products were run and visualized on a 1% agarose/ TBE gels stained with SYBR Safe, purified with Antarctic phosphatase (New England Biolabs, Beverly, MA The amplified products that did not show unique sequences were cloned. We used for cloning the pGEM-T Easy Vector System and high-efficiency competent cells (≥ 1×108 cfu/µg DNA) (Promega, www.promega.com). We carried out a 1:1 insert-to-vector molar ratio for the ligation. Transformation was performed using JM109 high-efficiency competent cells following the manufacturer's instructions. We selected sixteen colonyforming units (cfu) from each plate and recovered inserts were amplified using modified M13 primers OMNI (5'-ACAGG AAACAGCTATGACCATGAT-3') and UNI (5'-CGACGTTGT AAAACGAGGCCAGT-3'). Each PCR contained 2 µl NH4×10 buffer, 0.8 µl 50 mM MgCl2, 0.2 µl 25 mM dNTPs, 0.5 µl 10µM of each primer, 0.12 µl Taq DNA polymerase, 2 µl cloned product and 14.03 µl deionised water to complete a reaction volume of 20 µl. PCR thermal cycling conditions were as follows: 5 min at 94°C (longer than usual, to lyse bacteria), followed by 35 cycles of 30 s at 94°C, 30 s at 58°C, and 30 s at 72°C. The cycles ended with one final extension of 10 min at 72°C. Resulting amplicons were unidirectionally sequenced using the same forward primer.

div.head: Data Analysis
div.p: In this study we investigated the effects on the amplification success of prey DNA in bat scats of the time elapsed between faeces collection and DNA extraction (three to 12 years), conservation method (dried versus frozen) and DNA extraction method (two protocols). Additionally, we checked the efficiency of the specific amplification of avian DNA using different pairs of primers targeting cyt b and COI genes. To test the significance of all these effects on DNA amplification, we performed Generalized Linear Models (GLM) using the package 'MASS' of the program R (Venables and Ripley, 2002). Model construction followed a forward stepwise procedure and the selection was based on the percentage of deviance explained and the Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC), where smaller AIC values suggesting a better fit to data. The analysis was performed in two steps: we first tested for a determining influence on amplification by any of the selected factors using a binomial GLM with all treatments and 'DNA amplification' as dependent variable. Then, we tested for factors that influence the success in amplification of avian DNA considering only those treatments that yielded positive amplifications and using this time a negative binomial GLM according to the distribution of the data. For the second design, amplifications were considered as 'useful' only when the resulting sequences were recognized as being from one or more birds. Whereas amplifications of DNA from other organisms (including bats) and ambiguous sequences were considered as 'useless' as well as the null amplifications since these sequences could not be used in a direct species identification (without cloning).

div.head: RESULTS
div.p: We selected two primer pairs for the cyt b and one primer pair for COI that amplified fragments of 160 or 380 bp (Table 2). In the first analysis of DNA amplification success, most of the variation (66.6%) was explained by a model that included all the factors (storing time, conservation method, extraction protocol and pair of primers), although any of them had significant influence by itself. For the second analysis, based on positive amplifications only, the model with lower AIC and higher explanation of the variation (45.0%) included as significant factors 'preservation method', 'extraction protocol' and their interaction, and 'primers selection'. The factor 'storing time' was the one explaining the least percentage of variation (< 1%) and it was excluded of the model. The results showed statistically significant differences between extraction methods depending of the preservation method utilized (Table 3 and Fig. 1). Thus, the modified silica extraction with pulverization was statistically significant when the faeces had been dried, but not when they had been frozen (Z = -1.30, P = 0.19). On the other hand, the amplification rate of our designed primers was always higher than the amplification rate of vertebrate and bird generalist primers independent of the extraction method whereas there were no statistically significant differences in amplification success between the newly designed primers which, on the other hand, never targeted non-bird sequences (Table 3 and Fig. 2).

All bird DNA fragments amplified were reliably identified to species level, indicating that the sequences had a minimum of 4 bp differences between closely related species in the case of the cyt b fragments (2.5% in CytbSPreyFW/RW and1.1% in GCA GGC GGT TTT ATG TTG ATT GCT G CytbLPreyFW/RW, n = 81 sequences), and 9 bp in the case of the COI fragments (1.2% in BC-FW-13/BCV-RV1, 1.4% in Bird-F1/COIbirdR2 and 2.4% in COIPrey-FW/RW; n = 77 sequences) according to the absolute distance matrix obtained with PAUP for each primer set. From the total of 47 samples with only bird sequences only four (8.5%) presented double picks. These results indicated that there is no risk of misidentifying species when we compare the sequences in GenBank.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: Non-invasive techniques based on the amplification of genetic markers have proven to be very effective in diet studies, offering significantly greater resolution in prey identification than most of the traditional techniques (Symondson, 2002;Parsons et al., 2005;Deagle et al., 2007;King et al., 2008;Dun shea, 2009;Zeale et al., 2011). Together with the DNA of the consumed prey, faeces contain generally a mixture of DNAs originated from epithelial cells that cover the intestinal walls of the predator, and from bacteria, fungi and parasites among other sources. Nevertheless, the existence of multiple templates doesn't affect to the sequence determination since chimeras and were easily identified by eye-inspection or in the BLAST. On the other hand, the presence of different sequences in one single faeces, indicating the presence of more than one bird, was very rare in our sampling. In this study, bird DNA found in the excrements of noctule bats seems to be better preserved within the feather's rachis, which serves as a protective structure. This DNA is less susceptible to the effects of gastric acids, degradation by external agents and the effect of organisms (e.g., Farrell et al., 2000;Murphy et al., 2007;Haag et al., 2009;Brinkman et al., 2010). Therefore, the amplification of relatively larger fragments (160-380 bp) than those usually analyzed (100-250 bp) in diet studies (Pompanon et al., 2011) is more likely. In our analyses, the GuSCN-based extraction method with previous pulverization has proven to be more effective than This result is probably due to the fact that when pulverizing the faecal pellet, the within-rachis DNA is also extracted and made available. Besides, it is expected that this DNA will be in better conditions than other DNAs present in the faeces, and which amplification is highly dependent on preservation and extraction methods (Frantzen et al., 1998;Piggott and Taylor, 2003;Prugh et al., 2005). In the case of the modified Mini Kit of Qiagen without pulverization, only the DNA that remains more exposed is extracted and made available, whereas the DNA inside the rachis is not reached. This fact would explain why the conservation method has a significant effect on the amplification success only in combination with this extraction method. Thus, DNA amplification from material preserved frozen (and not pulverized) yields better results most probably due to less DNA degradation, than the amplification from dried-preserved material. Finally, storing time does not significantly influence DNA amplification success, probably because the period of time elapsed since the collection of the samples and their study was not long enough for significant differences in DNA's breakdown and despite possible limitations in the sampling.

The mtDNA markers cyt b and COI have been used extensively by mammalogists and ornithologists for species identification. At the beginning of this study, databases for cyt b were more extensive for birds than those for COI although the later has been favored by ornithologists due to the development of the DNA barcode and standardized reference libraries. In our study both cyt b and COI showed similar resolution. The whole idea of the paper was to design and test straightforward primers capable of amplifying only birds' DNA to allow a quick species identification. Vertebrate and avian generalist primers were only relatively efficient (25-38%) in the detection of avian DNA within the bat's faecal pellets. This was most probably due to their lower specificity and the relatively large size (for degraded DNA) of the fragments that they amplified. It is well known that smaller fragments survive better to digestion and are more detectable than larger ones (e.g., Sheppard and Harwood, 2005). Using the modified silica method extraction with pulverization and the designed primers, the success percentage was between 81-89% and none of the primers amplified bat's DNA. These amplification success values are quite satisfactory in relation to other studies. In fact, the percentage of predator DNA amplified from fresh scat samples of captive jaguars was 87% (Haag et al., 2009), 76.8% from dried scats of Andean cats (Napolitano et al., 2008), and 88% from scats of pine marten and stone marten stored in ethanol or frozen (Ruiz-González et al., 2008) and over 90% of bats (Boston et al., 2012).

The three fragments obtained with our designed primers showed similar efficiency and they can be used together for prey identification since the combination of two primer pairs increases the amplification success rate up to 100%, although the pair CytbSPreyFW/RW showed a wider range of amplification success percentages. The presented primers will reduce then the need for cloning only when two (or more) birds are found in the same faeces. We recommend combining the COI primer pair (COIPrey-FW/RW) with CytbLPreyFW/RW to ensure that at least one sequence can be found in the DNA databases. The length of the fragments would allow an easy DNA amplification by Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) techniques but in cases of extremely low sequence diversity like this one, it seems inappropriate.

The bird species selection used to study specificity is highly representative of the potential preys availability to the bats and since there were no ambiguous haplotypes in the chosen fragments for any of the potential preys, species identification will be unequivocal at least within the Iberian Peninsula. Due to their specificity and high amplification rate, it will be highly useful to check these new primers on a wider variety of test cases to establish their possible broader applicability for studying the small bird component in the diet of other predators in the Palaearctic, for example, of the other known bird-eating bats such as the great evening bat Ia io (Thabah et al., 2007), or the bird-like noctule Ny ctalus aviator (Fukui et al., 2013). This primer combination should work even for raptors such as the Eleonora's falcon (Falco eleonorae) and the sooty falcon (Falco concolor), which are the only two diurnal predators that show a similar predatory strategy than the giant noctule bat in the Mediterra nean region (Ibáñez et al., 2001). So far, bird identification in the diet studies of these raptors is based on the study of remains found near the nests, and this is not always possible (e.g., De León et al., 2007). Our primers would help identify unambiguously the species to which all the remains belong to.

In summary, the modified silica method with GuSCN binding solution (Rohland and Hofreiter, 2007), in which samples are frozen by liquid nitrogen and then pulverized, turned out to be more effective than DNA stool Mini Kit (Qiagen) when the faeces are not fresh, due to the fact that the DNA is extracted from feather remains protected of degradation inside the rachis. When using the modified silica with GuSCN extraction protocol, the conservation method used to store faecal samples as well as storing time do not affect amplification success due to the pulverization of the sample. Our designed primers allow amplify satisfactorily mtDNA fragments of birds consumed by the giant noctule bat and the identification of the bird species for all the samples. These primers will allow us to study in detail the avian diet composition of the poorly known giant noctule bat, unique in its partial carnivore diet in the entire European continent, and could be used in the diet analysis of other bird predators.
